extracted.intended_audience: students and educated readers of natural philosophy / historical biology
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook-style chapter explaining the 'law of evolution' as a general process of integration (concentration of matter) and dissipation of motion across astronomy, geology, biology, and embryology, illustrating when evolution is 'simple' or becomes 'compound'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions under which Evolution becomes compound
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution becomes compound where large amounts of secondary re-distribution are possible and these re-distributions attain permanence; this requires (1) a great quantity of contained motion to allow re-distributions and (2) conditions that prevent further re-distribution so the changes persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains that secondary re-distributions are possible only where there is much contained motion, yet permanence of these re-distributions requires the contained motion to be small (i.e., some solidification). The reconciliation of these apparently contradictory conditions (mobility to permit change, solidity to preserve it) is what allows highly compounded evolution, especially in organic aggregates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organic aggregates distinguished by combination of large contained motion with high concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Organic aggregates are peculiar because they combine an enormous amount of molecular motion locked up in small space with a high degree of concentration (semi-solid/plastic consistency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: three out of four chief components of organic matter are gaseous in isolation (hence high molecular motion); protein-molecules concentrate many equivalents of gaseous elements; colloid (not crystalloid) molecular aggregation; nitrogenous compounds absorb heat during formation, adding motion; water permeation supplies molecular mobility and plasticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence of secondary redistributions requires reconciliation of mobility and solidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary redistributions can have permanence only where further solidification stops further re-distribution, even though redistribution is only possible with sufficient contained motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central paradox resolved for compound evolution: systems must both allow internal rearrangements (motion) and also attain sufficient fixity for those rearrangements to be lasting. The text repeatedly emphasizes this reconciliation as key to organic complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of contained water correlates with capacity for secondary redistribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Other things equal, there is a direct relation between the amount of secondary redistribution an organism can undergo and its contained quantity of water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting examples: cutting off water supply arrests a plant's formative (secondary) changes; desiccated rotifera and Lepidosiren revive when wetted; young plants and eggs (more succulent) show faster structural change; within organisms, tissues with higher water ratio (shoot tips, brain) show faster change than dense dry tissues (trunk, nails, horns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of insensible motion (heat) correlates with structure and rate of structural change
rubrics_metrics.description: Amounts of structure and rates of structural change are correlated with the contained heat of organisms; higher internal temperature tends to accompany greater organic activity and complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative evidence: plants generally cooler and less structured than animals; vertebrates generally warmer and more complex than invertebrates; among vertebrates, fishes (similar temp to water) are least compounded, reptiles intermediate, birds and mammals hotter and more complex. Seasonal and experimental temperature effects on plants/ova/hibernation illustrate causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary vs. secondary redistribution: speed of primary redistribution determines simplicity vs. complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the primary redistribution (integration/concentration) is rapid, aggregates remain simple; where it is slow, secondary redistributions have time to accumulate and the result becomes compound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter frames evolution fundamentally as an integration of matter and dissipation of motion; whether the resulting aggregates are simple or compound depends on the relative rapidity of the primary (large-scale) redistribution versus the accumulation of secondary rearrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution defined as integration of matter and dissipation of motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Evolution (in the broad, philosophical sense used here) is always to be regarded as fundamentally an integration of Matter and dissipation of Motion, often accompanied by other transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeats this as the central law to be verified inductively across astronomy, geology, biology, psychology, and sociology. Instances: nebular condensation, formation of Earth's crust, organic growth, embryological development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local (secondary) integration accompanies primary integration and manifests as increasing subdivision and consolidation
rubrics_metrics.description: Along with forming a larger mass (primary integration), there is drawing together and consolidation of the matter into parts and increasingly intimate combination of parts (secondary/local integration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from embryology and development: heart twisting and integrating, bile-cells consolidating into liver, head formation by folding and union of anterior segments, post-natal ossification and coalescence of bones. These local integrations occur longitudinally and transversely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal integration (segment fusion) as evidence of evolutionary integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduction in number of serial segments and their fusion (longitudinal integration) across phylogeny and ontogeny indicates progression toward higher integration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: annelid/annulosa series—worms/myriapods with many segments vs higher crustaceans/insects with fewer and more integrated segments; lobster head+thorax box formation; vertebral coalescence in higher vertebrates (sacrum, coccyx). Parallels drawn between embryonic development and phylogenetic series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transverse integration (lateral coalescence into single structures) as evidence of evolutionary integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Consolidation of lateral paired structures into median single structures (transverse integration) is another mode of increasing integration in development and phylogeny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nervous system ganglia pairing becoming a single chain in higher annulosa; development of the brain from multiple cephalic ganglia; generative system duct convergence in mammals (from double uterus in some groups to single median structures in higher groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organismic growth as concentration of previously diffused elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Organisms grow by concentrating in themselves elements that were previously diffused (as gases) in the environment; the microscopic germ shows early evolution mainly as absorption of nutriment (primary integration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cells in an ovary becoming ova by growth at the expense of adjacent material; a fertilized ovum draws substance to a germinal centre; this illustrates primary integration prior to secondary differentiation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural modifiability correlates with tissue density, water content, and age
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity to acquire habits and aptitudes (structural modifiability) is higher in tissues and organisms with greater water content and lower density, and declines with age as water:solid ratio decreases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: young plants and embryos are more succulent and show faster change; children show greater structural modifiability than adults, adults more than old persons; within organisms, shoot tips and brain (more water) modify more rapidly than dry tissues like hair and nails.
